extraction.body: Running time: 174 minutes. Rated R (language and some graphic nudity). In theaters Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year. The Theranos founder with a husky voice and giant freaky eyes out of a Walter Keane painting has endlessly fascinated the world since her story was dramatized on the 2022 series “The Dropout” starring Amanda Seyfried. After that hit — a hit job in her estimation — Holmes became a party impression, a Halloween costume, an “SNL” joke and a dinner table topic. Whatever she is, most rational people believe that what she did — misleading the public and deep-pocketed investors that her “revolutionary” blood-testing device actually worked — was wrong. But not off-her-rocker Holmes and her equally delusional and sometimes downright villainous fiancé, Billy Evans, who we meet in this truly shocking and invasive film. This cuckoo couple’s credo is: innocent until well after proven guilty. Holmes, they say, is merely the victim of the court of public opinion. “Liz has been turned into this monster because nobody knows who she is,” Evans, lovable as a garden snake, says. Seizing a popular, touchy-feely word, he insists his betrothed has been “othered.” So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas. Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us. Watching “You Can See Everything” is like being on Willy Wonka’s messed-up boat for three unbelievable hours. If the pair’s aim was to show that Holmes is perfectly normal, um, whoops! Over and over she stares frighteningly into the distance as if about to say, “Mr. DeMille, I’m ready for my closeup.” Occasionally a single tear cascades down her cheek as in the recent horror flick “ Other Mommy .” Sorry, “ Othered Mommy.” And while they do get the “human story” they hoped awkward, uncomfortable Fielder would deliver, he’s a rather deft and dogged interviewer with a truffle hound’s nose for a story. “Have you ever lied in your life?” he smartly asks her. Holmes, less of a human than “E.T.,” replies, “I don’t think so.” Fielder and Oppenheim’s sometimes funny, frequently chilling, visually stunning flick is unusual, to say the least. This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was. This is an intrusive character study that, in a stimulating and riveting way, muddies the situation even more. We start to wonder: Has Holmes repeatedly fallen prey to bad men who take advantage of her charm, such as her ex-boyfriend and Theranos co-founder Sunny Balwani and, cough cough, others? Are her actions really their fault? Or does she gravitate toward those kinds of guys so they can act as an easy shield for her shrewd manipulations? Is she a nice girl led astray or a criminal mastermind? We’re even more mixed up as the camera’s focus goes to her adorable little children, a baby and a toddler. It’s hard not to feel sympathy for a young mother, or at least the kids who are about to be separated from her for more than a decade. If you know anything about prison, you know you can’t just take documentary cameras through the metal detector during visiting hours. So, once Holmes goes to the clink, Fielder and Oppenheim must get creative for the second half — resulting in some of the craziest stuff I’ve ever seen in a movie. Using transcripts from notes and memories, Fielder takes the old workhorse of documentary reenactments and gives it a novel twist. But what starts out as just a clever and fun idea warps into a dark, meta experiment that verges on a psychological thriller. If we were already questioning what’s real and what isn’t, it’s here when our brains explode and pool on the floor with the popcorn kernels and scattered Nerds. Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like. But midway through, we begin to positively loathe him. The man, who’s mystifyingly working to exhume Theranos from the start-up cemetery, is soon to be the planet’s jackass du jour. A flagrant narcissist, he asks the camera crew to come film him working out at the gym. And, lending credence to the title, at one point we watch him taking a shower totally naked with full-frontal. But he’s also slimy with his partner. As Holmes is beating eggs, he snatches the bowl away because he doesn’t like her whisking technique. When Fielder presses her on her shady verbiage — that her machine “can” perform hundreds of blood tests, as opposed to “is capable of” doing so with the right chemistry advancements — Evans condescendingly jumps in to say, “You were communicating very clearly in your mind.” But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question. Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year.

The Theranos founder with a husky voice and giant freaky eyes out of a Walter Keane painting has endlessly fascinated the world since her story was dramatized on the 2022 series “The Dropout” starring Amanda Seyfried.

After that hit — a hit job in her estimation — Holmes became a party impression, a Halloween costume, an “SNL” joke and a dinner table topic. Whatever she is, most rational people believe that what she did — misleading the public and deep-pocketed investors that her “revolutionary” blood-testing device actually worked — was wrong.

But not off-her-rocker Holmes and her equally delusional and sometimes downright villainous fiancé, Billy Evans, who we meet in this truly shocking and invasive film. This cuckoo couple’s credo is: innocent until well after proven guilty. Holmes, they say, is merely the victim of the court of public opinion.
“Liz has been turned into this monster because nobody knows who she is,” Evans, lovable as a garden snake, says. Seizing a popular, touchy-feely word, he insists his betrothed has been “othered.”

So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas. Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us. Watching “You Can See Everything” is like being on Willy Wonka’s messed-up boat for three unbelievable hours.

If the pair’s aim was to show that Holmes is perfectly normal, um, whoops! Over and over she stares frighteningly into the distance as if about to say, “Mr. DeMille, I’m ready for my closeup.” Occasionally a single tear cascades down her cheek as in the recent horror flick “ Other Mommy .” Sorry, “ Othered Mommy.” And while they do get the “human story” they hoped awkward, uncomfortable Fielder would deliver, he’s a rather deft and dogged interviewer with a truffle hound’s nose for a story.
“Have you ever lied in your life?” he smartly asks her.
Holmes, less of a human than “E.T.,” replies, “I don’t think so.”

Fielder and Oppenheim’s sometimes funny, frequently chilling, visually stunning flick is unusual, to say the least. This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was. This is an intrusive character study that, in a stimulating and riveting way, muddies the situation even more.

We start to wonder: Has Holmes repeatedly fallen prey to bad men who take advantage of her charm, such as her ex-boyfriend and Theranos co-founder Sunny Balwani and, cough cough, others? Are her actions really their fault? Or does she gravitate toward those kinds of guys so they can act as an easy shield for her shrewd manipulations? Is she a nice girl led astray or a criminal mastermind?

We’re even more mixed up as the camera’s focus goes to her adorable little children, a baby and a toddler. It’s hard not to feel sympathy for a young mother, or at least the kids who are about to be separated from her for more than a decade.

If you know anything about prison, you know you can’t just take documentary cameras through the metal detector during visiting hours. So, once Holmes goes to the clink, Fielder and Oppenheim must get creative for the second half — resulting in some of the craziest stuff I’ve ever seen in a movie.

Using transcripts from notes and memories, Fielder takes the old workhorse of documentary reenactments and gives it a novel twist. But what starts out as just a clever and fun idea warps into a dark, meta experiment that verges on a psychological thriller. If we were already questioning what’s real and what isn’t, it’s here when our brains explode and pool on the floor with the popcorn kernels and scattered Nerds.

Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like. But midway through, we begin to positively loathe him. The man, who’s mystifyingly working to exhume Theranos from the start-up cemetery, is soon to be the planet’s jackass du jour. A flagrant narcissist, he asks the camera crew to come film him working out at the gym. And, lending credence to the title, at one point we watch him taking a shower totally naked with full-frontal. But he’s also slimy with his partner.

As Holmes is beating eggs, he snatches the bowl away because he doesn’t like her whisking technique. When Fielder presses her on her shady verbiage — that her machine “can” perform hundreds of blood tests, as opposed to “is capable of” doing so with the right chemistry advancements — Evans condescendingly jumps in to say, “You were communicating very clearly in your mind.”

But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question. Fans of reality TV know that a season’s hero and the baddie can be determined, or at least amplified, in the editing room. And at the end of “You Can See Everything,” Fielder and Oppenheim suggest that perhaps our trusty interviewer liked one of these two more than the other, and that preference seeped into his subconscious.
Ding! Isn’t that exactly how this bewitching and fascinating woman became the youngest-ever self-made billionaire in the first place?

coreStoryFacts.text: “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes.
We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent.
What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong.

Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered.
In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself.
But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth.
Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there.
“I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.”
No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche.
“If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes.
The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas.
Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a significant role in one of the most talked-about movies of the year.
With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to recall Holmes’ exact phrasing and delivery.
Meet scaling and investment leaders, ask questions, find solutions, and more.
AI agents are coming to Rivian’s cars Sean O'Kane
Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage.
In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas.
Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted.
Evans knows that Fielder and Oppenheim are not convinced of Holmes’ innocence.

One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is. “I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.” No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral , Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble. “If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes. “I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.” We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered. Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore. In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas. “The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.” Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up. And yet, Holmes and her husband, hotel heir Billy Evans, were livid about the article. At one point in an interview, Holmes tells the Times reporter that she wasn’t offended by actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in Hulu’s miniseries “ The Dropout ” because “they’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” She and her husband insist that the quote was taken out of context. They claim that they have evidence that Holmes actually said, “They’re playing a character they created,” relieving her from any implication that she admitted to concocting an inauthentic persona as CEO of Theranos. Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted. He never does. He calls in the perfect sidekick to help him dissect her confounding behavior: the very actress who portrays her in “The Dropout.” Fielder plays Seyfried a brutal clip from his time with Holmes, when he tries watching “The Dropout” with the subject of the series. When they get to a tense scene involving Holmes’ manipulative ex-boyfriend and former Theranos partner in crime Sunny Balwani — who is also now in prison — Holmes can no longer bear to watch this fictional version of herself. She turns away and cries. In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself. passages: “Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes.

One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is.
“I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.”

No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral , Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble.
“If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes.
“I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.”

sources.title: 'You Can See Everything' review: Wild Elizabeth Holmes doc is one of the craziest movies I've ever seen - New York Post
passages: Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year.

So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas.
Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us.
But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question.
Fans of reality TV know that a season’s hero and the baddie can be determined, or at least amplified, in the editing room.
This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was.
Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like.

extraction.body: Running time: 174 minutes. Rated R (language and some graphic nudity). In theaters Movies don’t come much wilder than “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s brilliant, up-close-and-personal documentary about convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes that’s already the talker of the year. The Theranos founder with a husky voice and giant freaky eyes out of a Walter Keane painting has endlessly fascinated the world since her story was dramatized on the 2022 series “The Dropout” starring Amanda Seyfried. After that hit — a hit job in her estimation — Holmes became a party impression, a Halloween costume, an “SNL” joke and a dinner table topic. Whatever she is, most rational people believe that what she did — misleading the public and deep-pocketed investors that her “revolutionary” blood-testing device actually worked — was wrong. But not off-her-rocker Holmes and her equally delusional and sometimes downright villainous fiancé, Billy Evans, who we meet in this truly shocking and invasive film. This cuckoo couple’s credo is: innocent until well after proven guilty. Holmes, they say, is merely the victim of the court of public opinion. “Liz has been turned into this monster because nobody knows who she is,” Evans, lovable as a garden snake, says. Seizing a popular, touchy-feely word, he insists his betrothed has been “othered.” So, he and Holmes invite oddball comedian Fielder of all people into their beach house rental in San Diego, Calif., to document the 34 days before she begins her 11-year prison sentence in Bryan, Texas. Well, that bizarre choice has backfired for them, but it’s a seismically entertaining coup for us. Watching “You Can See Everything” is like being on Willy Wonka’s messed-up boat for three unbelievable hours. If the pair’s aim was to show that Holmes is perfectly normal, um, whoops! Over and over she stares frighteningly into the distance as if about to say, “Mr. DeMille, I’m ready for my closeup.” Occasionally a single tear cascades down her cheek as in the recent horror flick “ Other Mommy .” Sorry, “ Othered Mommy.” And while they do get the “human story” they hoped awkward, uncomfortable Fielder would deliver, he’s a rather deft and dogged interviewer with a truffle hound’s nose for a story. “Have you ever lied in your life?” he smartly asks her. Holmes, less of a human than “E.T.,” replies, “I don’t think so.” Fielder and Oppenheim’s sometimes funny, frequently chilling, visually stunning flick is unusual, to say the least. This is not a doc of straightforward revelations such as those of “The Jinx.” Nor is it a clear rundown of events, like the Holmes movie “ The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley ” was. This is an intrusive character study that, in a stimulating and riveting way, muddies the situation even more. We start to wonder: Has Holmes repeatedly fallen prey to bad men who take advantage of her charm, such as her ex-boyfriend and Theranos co-founder Sunny Balwani and, cough cough, others? Are her actions really their fault? Or does she gravitate toward those kinds of guys so they can act as an easy shield for her shrewd manipulations? Is she a nice girl led astray or a criminal mastermind? We’re even more mixed up as the camera’s focus goes to her adorable little children, a baby and a toddler. It’s hard not to feel sympathy for a young mother, or at least the kids who are about to be separated from her for more than a decade. If you know anything about prison, you know you can’t just take documentary cameras through the metal detector during visiting hours. So, once Holmes goes to the clink, Fielder and Oppenheim must get creative for the second half — resulting in some of the craziest stuff I’ve ever seen in a movie. Using transcripts from notes and memories, Fielder takes the old workhorse of documentary reenactments and gives it a novel twist. But what starts out as just a clever and fun idea warps into a dark, meta experiment that verges on a psychological thriller. If we were already questioning what’s real and what isn’t, it’s here when our brains explode and pool on the floor with the popcorn kernels and scattered Nerds. Most of Fielder’s time is spent from here on out with Evans, who we never like. But midway through, we begin to positively loathe him. The man, who’s mystifyingly working to exhume Theranos from the start-up cemetery, is soon to be the planet’s jackass du jour. A flagrant narcissist, he asks the camera crew to come film him working out at the gym. And, lending credence to the title, at one point we watch him taking a shower totally naked with full-frontal. But he’s also slimy with his partner. As Holmes is beating eggs, he snatches the bowl away because he doesn’t like her whisking technique. When Fielder presses her on her shady verbiage — that her machine “can” perform hundreds of blood tests, as opposed to “is capable of” doing so with the right chemistry advancements — Evans condescendingly jumps in to say, “You were communicating very clearly in your mind.” But Fielder even calls our antipathy toward Evans into question. Fans of reality TV know that a season’s hero and the baddie can be determined, or at least amplified, in the editing room. And at the end of “You Can See Everything,” Fielder and Oppenheim suggest that perhaps our trusty interviewer liked one of these two more than the other, and that preference seeped into his subconscious. Ding! Isn’t that exactly how this bewitching and fascinating woman became the youngest-ever self-made billionaire in the first place? The ultimate takeaway of this absolutely sensational, reality-bending, unmissable documentary? With Elizabeth Holmes, we will never see everything.

sources.title: Israeli spyware targeted 'hundreds of millions' through zero-click ads, researchers find - Middle East Eye
passages: Millions of people's devices have been infected with Israeli commercial spyware called Candiru through zero-click digital advertisements, Canadian cyber watchdog group The Citizen Lab found in an investigation .

Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report.
Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021.
The case marks the first zero-click mercenary spyware, confirmed publicly, delivered through targeted ads, the group said in a report published on Thursday.
The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network.
ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict".

Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it.
The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020.

extraction.body: Millions of people's devices have been infected with Israeli commercial spyware called Candiru through zero-click digital advertisements, Canadian cyber watchdog group The Citizen Lab found in an investigation . The case marks the first zero-click mercenary spyware, confirmed publicly, delivered through targeted ads, the group said in a report published on Thursday. The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network. Mercenary spyware is a highly advanced, custom-built form of malware created by private companies and sold to paying clients, including states. Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report. The Citizen Lab found that in 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in a series of zero-click ad attacks purchased by Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it. During a four-month period, Discover-Tech's ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Aside from Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, Discover-Tech is also linked to other mercenary spyware actors, including Intelos and Bindecy. Candiru was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 for "engaging in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States". Candiru's rebrand came after it was acquired by US private equity firm Integrity Partners in 2025, which is not sanctioned by the US. Discover-Tech has appeared as a "certified and "approved" vendor operated by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has placed ads in major networks including Google, the Russian search engine Yandex and the platform Beeswax. "The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at The Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike." Jerome Dangu, cofounder of the New York advertising security firm Confiant, which also published a separate report on the case on Thursday, said that Discover-Tech was placing at least 10 million ads per day worldwide and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond its advertisements' reach. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Dangu added that the ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. The Citizen Lab said it had also found Discover-Tech ad impressions in Nato and United Nations networks, as well as the European Parliament, European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. Ads also appeared in media organisations in eight countries including Australia, Mexico and Europe. Israeli spyware firm NSO Group was also added to the US trade blacklist, along with Candiru, in November 2021, after the US concluded that foreign governments had bought its spyware and used it to target government officials, journalists, and others. Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021. The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020. The campaign targeted 20 other websites in two waves: April to July 2020 and January to August 2021. ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict". Following findings by the two research groups, Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, and other platforms have since disconnected Discover-Tech's access to the digital advertising market. Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report.
The Citizen Lab found that in 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in a series of zero-click ad attacks purchased by Discover-Tech.

Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it.
During a four-month period, Discover-Tech's ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries.
Aside from Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, Discover-Tech is also linked to other mercenary spyware actors, including Intelos and Bindecy.

Candiru was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 for "engaging in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States". Candiru's rebrand came after it was acquired by US private equity firm Integrity Partners in 2025, which is not sanctioned by the US.

Discover-Tech has appeared as a "certified and "approved" vendor operated by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has placed ads in major networks including Google, the Russian search engine Yandex and the platform Beeswax.

"The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at The Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike."

Jerome Dangu, cofounder of the New York advertising security firm Confiant, which also published a separate report on the case on Thursday, said that Discover-Tech was placing at least 10 million ads per day worldwide and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond its advertisements' reach.

"Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Dangu added that the ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court.

The Citizen Lab said it had also found Discover-Tech ad impressions in Nato and United Nations networks, as well as the European Parliament, European Commission and more than a dozen national governments.
Ads also appeared in media organisations in eight countries including Australia, Mexico and Europe.

Israeli spyware firm NSO Group was also added to the US trade blacklist, along with Candiru, in November 2021, after the US concluded that foreign governments had bought its spyware and used it to target government officials, journalists, and others.
Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021.

The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020. The campaign targeted 20 other websites in two waves: April to July 2020 and January to August 2021.
ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict".
Following findings by the two research groups, Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, and other platforms have since disconnected Discover-Tech's access to the digital advertising market.

extraction.body: A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part. Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found. You are not even required to “click” on anything. An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims. In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files. An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks. Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera. “This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.” Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners. Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries. Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable. Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera. “To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities. “The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said. Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials. It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time. Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect. While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection. Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on. “Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.” “Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added. Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax. In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse. Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found. The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat. Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab. In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.” The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said. Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

extraction.body: Millions of people's devices have been infected with Israeli commercial spyware called Candiru through zero-click digital advertisements, Canadian cyber watchdog group The Citizen Lab found in an investigation . The case marks the first zero-click mercenary spyware, confirmed publicly, delivered through targeted ads, the group said in a report published on Thursday. The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network. Mercenary spyware is a highly advanced, custom-built form of malware created by private companies and sold to paying clients, including states. Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report. The Citizen Lab found that in 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in a series of zero-click ad attacks purchased by Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it. During a four-month period, Discover-Tech's ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Aside from Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, Discover-Tech is also linked to other mercenary spyware actors, including Intelos and Bindecy. Candiru was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 for "engaging in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States". Candiru's rebrand came after it was acquired by US private equity firm Integrity Partners in 2025, which is not sanctioned by the US. Discover-Tech has appeared as a "certified and "approved" vendor operated by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has placed ads in major networks including Google, the Russian search engine Yandex and the platform Beeswax. "The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at The Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike." Jerome Dangu, cofounder of the New York advertising security firm Confiant, which also published a separate report on the case on Thursday, said that Discover-Tech was placing at least 10 million ads per day worldwide and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond its advertisements' reach. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Dangu added that the ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. The Citizen Lab said it had also found Discover-Tech ad impressions in Nato and United Nations networks, as well as the European Parliament, European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. Ads also appeared in media organisations in eight countries including Australia, Mexico and Europe. Israeli spyware firm NSO Group was also added to the US trade blacklist, along with Candiru, in November 2021, after the US concluded that foreign governments had bought its spyware and used it to target government officials, journalists, and others. Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021. The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020. The campaign targeted 20 other websites in two waves: April to July 2020 and January to August 2021. ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict". Following findings by the two research groups, Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, and other platforms have since disconnected Discover-Tech's access to the digital advertising market. Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found. You are not even required to “click” on anything. An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims. In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files. An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks. Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera. “This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.” Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners. Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries. Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable. Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera. “To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities. “The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said. Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials. It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time. Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect. While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection. Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on. “Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.” “Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added. Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax. In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse. Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found. The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat. Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab. In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.” The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said. Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

relevantPassages.text: An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims.
Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat.
“We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera.
Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru.

The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries.
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024.
Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed.
Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found.
Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance.
“Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.”
A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part.
The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets.

Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners.

In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.

MSCI ( NYSE: MSCI ), a well-known index provider followed by many passive investment funds, plans to classify companies like Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR ) as "non-operating." This change would make them ineligible for MSCI's global indexes. As a result, Strategy could end up on a potential deletions list alongside Japan's Metaplanet, with final decisions expected by November 11, 2026, and removals starting on November 30. After the news, Strategy's stock fell 9.6% to $137 on October 16 and has dropped 11.4% over the past week. Meanwhile, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) remained relatively stable, slipping just 1.0% in the 24 hours leading up to October 16 to $81,548. So, how might this index decision, concerning the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, impact Bitcoin's price? The controversy began with an MSCI proposal that would have excluded any company whose digital asset holdings made up more than 50% of its total assets. Strategy voiced strong opposition, describing this threshold as "discriminatory towards digital assets" and "arbitrary," according to Chief Financial Officer Andrew Kang during a February 5 earnings call. Though MSCI retracted this proposal in January, the provider eventually initiated a broader consultation that led to the current "non-operating assets" test driving the potential removals. Strategy formally opposed the test, with Kang insisting that Strategy is "an operating company with a treasury balance sheet built upon a commodity," highlighting its 1,500-employee workforce and 2025 revenue of $477 million. While the company's software division generates consistent revenue—reporting $122.4 million in the second quarter (up 6.9% from the previous year), with subscription services growing by 54% to $62.9 million—most investors hold shares in Strategy primarily for its Bitcoin assets. The company holds 848,250 BTC, valued at about $69 billion at the current Bitcoin price, exceeding its $55.25 billion market cap. However, the second quarter also posted a substantial net loss of $8.22 billion, mainly due to an $8.32 billion unrealized loss on Bitcoin, as fair value accounting requires the company to mark its holdings to market every quarter. Index funds are passive investments that mirror the holdings of the indexes they track. If Strategy is removed from the index, index funds would be required to sell their shares, which could trigger about $2.8 billion in forced selling, according to JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE: JPM ). While this selling would affect MSTR shares, it wouldn't directly impact Bitcoin. The shares would change hands between buyers and sellers, so Strategy would retain custody of its Bitcoin. Bitcoin prices would only be affected if the company decided to sell some of its holdings, and the current MSCI terms don't obligate any company to do so. Michael Saylor, Strategy's executive chairman, expressed that the MSCI decision is "not that important to us," adding that MSCI manages "a fairly de minimis amount of capital." However, this perspective is expected, given that Saylor represents a company that could lose its index status. Traders, for their part, treated the news as a serious threat. The main link between Strategy's stock and Bitcoin is the company's buying power. Strategy has heavily invested in Bitcoin, funding purchases through the sale of new shares and preferred stock. In the second quarter alone, it raised $8.41 billion through "at-the-market" offerings. In 2025, it raised $25.3 billion. If the stock price declines and fewer index funds hold the shares, raising money could become more challenging. Strategy might need to issue a greater number of shares to acquire the same amount of Bitcoin. Furthermore, with an S&P credit rating of B-, far below investment grade, the company faces higher borrowing costs and limited access to bond funds that only deal in highly rated debt. Additionally, Strategy has recently begun selling some of its Bitcoin. The company's board approved sales of up to $1.25 billion to support its USD Reserve, and it has already sold $218.4 million of Bitcoin this year. The reserve currently stands at $3.75 billion, enough to cover more than 2.1 years of preferred dividends and interest on its $6.7 billion in convertible debt. However, the pressure on Bitcoin prices remains. Strategy's average purchase price is around $75,444 per Bitcoin, and Bitcoin's current $81,548 is only about 8% above it, while it trades 35.3% below its record high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. That said, Saylor previously reassured investors that falling below that cost threshold would not trigger any major actions, stating that Strategy has no "covenants or triggers" tied to its purchase price. The MSCI change is primarily an issue for Strategy's stock rather than Bitcoin directly. Bitcoin's price may be affected only if the company significantly slows its buying or decides to sell its Bitcoin assets in the future. The first clear test comes with MSCI's final list on November 11. If Strategy is on it and its reports after the November 30 removals show Bitcoin sales beyond the $218.4 million already sold this year, the index exit has reached the coin. MSCI ( NYSE: MSCI | MSCI Price Prediction ), a well-known index provider followed by many passive investment funds, plans to classify companies like Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR ) as “non-operating.” This change would make them ineligible for MSCI’s global indexes. As a result, Strategy could end up on a potential deletions list alongside Japan’s Metaplanet, with final decisions expected by November 11, 2026, and removals starting on November 30.

After the news, Strategy’s stock fell 9.6% to $137 on October 16 and has dropped 11.4% over the past week. Meanwhile, Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) remained relatively stable , slipping just 1.0% in the 24 hours leading up to October 16 to $81,548. So, how might this index decision, concerning the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin , impact Bitcoin’s price?

The controversy began with an MSCI proposal that would have excluded any company whose digital asset holdings made up more than 50% of its total assets. Strategy voiced strong opposition, describing this threshold as “discriminatory towards digital assets” and “arbitrary,” according to Chief Financial Officer Andrew Kang during a February 5 earnings call.

Though MSCI retracted this proposal in January, the provider eventually initiated a broader consultation that led to the current “non-operating assets” test driving the potential removals. Strategy formally opposed the test, with Kang insisting that Strategy is “an operating company with a treasury balance sheet built upon a commodity,” highlighting its 1,500-employee workforce and 2025 revenue of $477 million.

While the company’s software division generates consistent revenue—reporting $122.4 million in the second quarter (up 6.9% from the previous year), with subscription services growing by 54% to $62.9 million—most investors hold shares in Strategy primarily for its Bitcoin assets. The company holds 848,250 BTC, valued at about $69 billion at the current Bitcoin price, exceeding its $55.25 billion market cap.

However, the second quarter also posted a substantial net loss of $8.22 billion, mainly due to an $8.32 billion unrealized loss on Bitcoin, as fair value accounting requires the company to mark its holdings to market every quarter.

Index funds are passive investments that mirror the holdings of the indexes they track. If Strategy is removed from the index, index funds would be required to sell their shares, which could trigger about $2.8 billion in forced selling, according to JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE: JPM ).

While this selling would affect MSTR shares, it wouldn’t directly impact Bitcoin. The shares would change hands between buyers and sellers, so Strategy would retain custody of its Bitcoin. Bitcoin prices would only be affected if the company decided to sell some of its holdings, and the current MSCI terms don’t obligate any company to do so.

Michael Saylor, Strategy’s executive chairman, expressed that the MSCI decision is “not that important to us,” adding that MSCI manages “a fairly de minimis amount of capital.” However, this perspective is expected, given that Saylor represents a company that could lose its index status. Traders, for their part, treated the news as a serious threat.

The main link between Strategy’s stock and Bitcoin is the company’s buying power. Strategy has heavily invested in Bitcoin, funding purchases through the sale of new shares and preferred stock. In the second quarter alone, it raised $8.41 billion through “at-the-market” offerings. In 2025, it raised $25.3 billion.

If the stock price declines and fewer index funds hold the shares, raising money could become more challenging. Strategy might need to issue a greater number of shares to acquire the same amount of Bitcoin. Furthermore, with an S&P credit rating of B-, far below investment grade, the company faces higher borrowing costs and limited access to bond funds that only deal in highly rated debt.

Additionally, Strategy has recently begun selling some of its Bitcoin. The company’s board approved sales of up to $1.25 billion to support its USD Reserve, and it has already sold $218.4 million of Bitcoin this year. The reserve currently stands at $3.75 billion, enough to cover more than 2.1 years of preferred dividends and interest on its $6.7 billion in convertible debt.

However, the pressure on Bitcoin prices remains. Strategy’s average purchase price is around $75,444 per Bitcoin, and Bitcoin’s current $81,548 is only about 8% above it, while it trades 35.3% below its record high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. That said, Saylor previously reassured investors that falling below that cost threshold would not trigger any major actions, stating that Strategy has no “covenants or triggers” tied to its purchase price.

The MSCI change is primarily an issue for Strategy’s stock rather than Bitcoin directly. Bitcoin’s price may be affected only if the company significantly slows its buying or decides to sell its Bitcoin assets in the future.

The first clear test comes with MSCI’s final list on November 11. If Strategy is on it and its reports after the November 30 removals show Bitcoin sales beyond the $218.4 million already sold this year, the index exit has reached the coin. If its purchases keep coming instead, the damage stays with MSTR shareholders.

MSCI ( NYSE: MSCI ), a well-known index provider followed by many passive investment funds, plans to classify companies like Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR ) as "non-operating." This change would make them ineligible for MSCI's global indexes. As a result, Strategy could end up on a potential deletions list alongside Japan's Metaplanet, with final decisions expected by November 11, 2026, and removals starting on November 30. After the news, Strategy's stock fell 9.6% to $137 on October 16 and has dropped 11.4% over the past week. Meanwhile, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) remained relatively stable, slipping just 1.0% in the 24 hours leading up to October 16 to $81,548. So, how might this index decision, concerning the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, impact Bitcoin's price? The controversy began with an MSCI proposal that would have excluded any company whose digital asset holdings made up more than 50% of its total assets. Strategy voiced strong opposition, describing this threshold as "discriminatory towards digital assets" and "arbitrary," according to Chief Financial Officer Andrew Kang during a February 5 earnings call. Though MSCI retracted this proposal in January, the provider eventually initiated a broader consultation that led to the current "non-operating assets" test driving the potential removals. Strategy formally opposed the test, with Kang insisting that Strategy is "an operating company with a treasury balance sheet built upon a commodity," highlighting its 1,500-employee workforce and 2025 revenue of $477 million. While the company's software division generates consistent revenue—reporting $122.4 million in the second quarter (up 6.9% from the previous year), with subscription services growing by 54% to $62.9 million—most investors hold shares in Strategy primarily for its Bitcoin assets. The company holds 848,250 BTC, valued at about $69 billion at the current Bitcoin price, exceeding its $55.25 billion market cap. However, the second quarter also posted a substantial net loss of $8.22 billion, mainly due to an $8.32 billion unrealized loss on Bitcoin, as fair value accounting requires the company to mark its holdings to market every quarter. Index funds are passive investments that mirror the holdings of the indexes they track. If Strategy is removed from the index, index funds would be required to sell their shares, which could trigger about $2.8 billion in forced selling, according to JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE: JPM ). While this selling would affect MSTR shares, it wouldn't directly impact Bitcoin. The shares would change hands between buyers and sellers, so Strategy would retain custody of its Bitcoin. Bitcoin prices would only be affected if the company decided to sell some of its holdings, and the current MSCI terms don't obligate any company to do so. Michael Saylor, Strategy's executive chairman, expressed that the MSCI decision is "not that important to us," adding that MSCI manages "a fairly de minimis amount of capital." However, this perspective is expected, given that Saylor represents a company that could lose its index status. Traders, for their part, treated the news as a serious threat. The main link between Strategy's stock and Bitcoin is the company's buying power. Strategy has heavily invested in Bitcoin, funding purchases through the sale of new shares and preferred stock. In the second quarter alone, it raised $8.41 billion through "at-the-market" offerings. In 2025, it raised $25.3 billion. If the stock price declines and fewer index funds hold the shares, raising money could become more challenging. Strategy might need to issue a greater number of shares to acquire the same amount of Bitcoin. Furthermore, with an S&P credit rating of B-, far below investment grade, the company faces higher borrowing costs and limited access to bond funds that only deal in highly rated debt. Additionally, Strategy has recently begun selling some of its Bitcoin. The company's board approved sales of up to $1.25 billion to support its USD Reserve, and it has already sold $218.4 million of Bitcoin this year. The reserve currently stands at $3.75 billion, enough to cover more than 2.1 years of preferred dividends and interest on its $6.7 billion in convertible debt. However, the pressure on Bitcoin prices remains. Strategy's average purchase price is around $75,444 per Bitcoin, and Bitcoin's current $81,548 is only about 8% above it, while it trades 35.3% below its record high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. That said, Saylor previously reassured investors that falling below that cost threshold would not trigger any major actions, stating that Strategy has no "covenants or triggers" tied to its purchase price. The MSCI change is primarily an issue for Strategy's stock rather than Bitcoin directly. Bitcoin's price may be affected only if the company significantly slows its buying or decides to sell its Bitcoin assets in the future. The first clear test comes with MSCI's final list on November 11. If Strategy is on it and its reports after the November 30 removals show Bitcoin sales beyond the $218.4 million already sold this year, the index exit has reached the coin. passages: Crypto traders often call October "Uptober" because Bitcoin typically finishes the month with gains.
Since 2013, it has closed with losses only twice before 2025: in 2014 and 2018.
However, last year proved the trend could break, as Bitcoin ended October 2025 below its starting price.
Traders tend to buy Bitcoin early in the month when they anticipate an upswing, which can lead to price increases at the start of October.
Conversely, if October begins weakly, those expectations can prompt quick selling, which may push prices down further.
As we reach the midpoint of October 2026, Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) has dropped roughly 4%, putting its annual "Uptober" trend at risk once again.
As of October 12, Bitcoin is trading around $83,400, down from its September close of nearly $87,000.
Ultimately, the Uptober record offers little insight into how October 2026 will end.

A Bitcoin closing price above about $87,000 could keep the Uptober tradition alive for another year, while a close below that would mark a second consecutive October in the red, further diminishing the significance of the "Uptober" label.
Over the past week, every major cryptocurrency has fallen, with Bitcoin down 3%.
Bitcoin's positive months have consistently outnumbered negative months over about a dozen years, contributing to the nickname's popularity.
Moreover, no specific event or trigger in October guarantees strong Bitcoin performance.

Additionally, the record itself can influence trading behavior. Conversely, if October begins weakly, those expectations can prompt quick selling, which may push prices down further. This self-reinforcing cycle can weaken the reliability of the Uptober forecast.

Over the past week, every major cryptocurrency has fallen, with Bitcoin down 3%. Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) fell 6%, XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) fell 7.3%, Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) fell 7.6%, and Dogecoin (CRYPTO:DOGE) fell 9.7%.

Interestingly, the extent of each coin's drop reflects trader behavior. Generally, smaller coins tend to fall more sharply during risk-off weeks, when traders sell their more speculative assets first. This trend stands in contrast to September, when there was a noticeable rotation into altcoins.

All five coins bounced in the last 24 hours, with Bitcoin up 0.5%, Ethereum up 2.2%, XRP up 0.8%, Solana up 2%, and Dogecoin up 2.1%. However, it's important to remain cautious with short-term gains, as sellers can quickly run low on inventory after a rough week, allowing bargain hunters to step in and drive prices up. A genuine recovery often requires multiple days of consistently higher closing prices.

For October 2026 to end on a positive note, Bitcoin must close the month above its September figure of nearly $87,000. That means it needs to regain about 4% of what it has lost so far. Given Bitcoin's volatility, a quick turnaround is possible, especially with over two weeks left in the month.

In the bigger picture, Bitcoin faces a considerable climb, trading about 34% below its all-time high of $126,080. Recent short-term gains may signal either a recovery in a positive month or the start of a longer decline. The upcoming trading period will be crucial in determining the true direction.

Ultimately, the Uptober record offers little insight into how October 2026 will end. It reflects past performance over a limited timeframe without a clear cause-and-effect relationship. extraction.body: A 17-year-old is facing a murder charge after allegedly shooting a man in the head during a confrontation early Sunday morning, according to an arrest warrant affidavit.Maverik Parish, 17, was identified in court documents as the suspect in the death of 28-year-old Enrique Avila. The shooting happened around 2 a.m. on March 15 at 1900 East Long Ave.According to the affidavit filed by Fort Worth police, Parish was a passenger in a black 2004 Ford Expedition and had been firing a tan handgun into the ground several times before the encounter. Investigators say Avila, who reportedly appeared intoxicated and possibly having a schizophrenic episode, approached the SUV at the intersection of East Long and Schwartz avenues because he was upset that Parish had been firing a weapon in the neighborhood.Witnesses and occupants of the vehicle told police that Avila was unarmed and stood on the left side of the SUV, yelling at Parish through the passenger window. When the driver reversed and tried to drive around Avila, he moved into the vehicle's path, forcing it to stop again.As Avila walked toward the front of the vehicle, the affidavit alleges that Parish stuck the tan pistol out of the window and fired one shot. Avila collapsed in a grassy median and died at the scene.The occupants of the vehicle initially left the scene but then made a U-turn to return and check if the man had been shot. Officers, alerted by the Real Time Crime Center, conducted an investigatory stop in the 2900 block of North Nichols and detained all five people inside the vehicle. Police found a black pistol and a tan pistol in plain view inside the vehicle.The investigating detective noted that no witnesses believed Avila was armed or attempting to assault anyone, saying Parish used deadly force despite not being threatened with imminent harm.Parish remains in custody on a murder charge.

extraction.body: Millbrook Magnet High School had a very unexpected and special delivery on Thursday morning after the school's security officer went into labor. Principal Monica Sawyer and bookkeeper K'Mani Freeman heard the call for help and quickly jumped into action. "We got a call go out on our radios that said that there was a medical emergency in one of our bathrooms," Sawyer said. Freeman says she’s a Douala and instructed the principal what to do. She says the baby arrived within minutes. "I was like, well, we have a baby. Great, we probably need to warm her up just a little bit," Freeman said. Sawyer said it's a moment she'll never forget. "I heard a baby was crying and Ms. Freeman was telling us to go get a blanket from our office," Sawyer said. "I thought Brook would be a beautiful name as an ode to Millbrook. But we don't know. Mom hasn't decided yet," Sawyer said. In a letter to staff and families, Principal Sawyer said school staff stepped in to help deliver a beautiful baby girl on campus that morning. "We’re happy to share that both mom and baby are doing well," Sawyer said. "I know you’ll join me in congratulating the family and welcoming our newest (and tiniest!) Wildcat. We’ve already ordered some baby spirit wear so mom and daughter will be ready to cheer on the Wildcats together!" The school has set up a page to help support the newborn and family at this link. "What a special day to be a Wildcat!" Sawyer said.

passages: At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did.
As part of updates announced Friday, Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps.
Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved.
The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors.

The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors. Apple didn’t pull X or Grok from the App Store, though it told senators that it threatened to yank Grok. At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did. As part of updates announced Friday, Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps. Developers who “fail to implement adequate safeguards” or “don’t remedy violations after notice” may be removed from the App Store. Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved. Apple’s rules also more clearly spell out that any apps that “facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children” will be pulled from the App Store and “blocked from alternative distribution.”

In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity.
