The spyware also targeted devices linked to Al Jazeera Media Network. Mercenary spyware is a highly advanced, custom-built form of malware created by private companies and sold to paying clients, including states. Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate ad company but in reality operates for Israeli spyware partners like Candiru, placed targeted ads that directed millions of devices in dozens of countries to contact Candiru's servers for tracking and reconnaissance, according to the report. The Citizen Lab found that in 2024 and 2025, at least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in a series of zero-click ad attacks purchased by Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech controls a platform called Controlium that allows "mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices" as soon as the ad is shown, without having the target even click on it. During a four-month period, Discover-Tech's ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Aside from Candiru, rebranded as Integrity Labs, Discover-Tech is also linked to other mercenary spyware actors, including Intelos and Bindecy. Candiru was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 for "engaging in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States". Candiru's rebrand came after it was acquired by US private equity firm Integrity Partners in 2025, which is not sanctioned by the US. Discover-Tech has appeared as a "certified and "approved" vendor operated by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has placed ads in major networks including Google, the Russian search engine Yandex and the platform Beeswax. "The way online advertising works today is a systemic security threat," Wolfie Cristl, a senior researcher at The Citizen Lab, told Reuters. "For states, the private sector, civil society and everyone else alike." Jerome Dangu, cofounder of the New York advertising security firm Confiant, which also published a separate report on the case on Thursday, said that Discover-Tech was placing at least 10 million ads per day worldwide and that data-sharing arrangements - called cookie matching - allowed it to track people even beyond its advertisements' reach. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," Dangu said. Dangu added that the ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive categories," including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court. The Citizen Lab said it had also found Discover-Tech ad impressions in Nato and United Nations networks, as well as the European Parliament, European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. Ads also appeared in media organisations in eight countries including Australia, Mexico and Europe. Israeli spyware firm NSO Group was also added to the US trade blacklist, along with Candiru, in November 2021, after the US concluded that foreign governments had bought its spyware and used it to target government officials, journalists, and others. Candiru was also used to target Middle East Eye and other websites in November 2021. The attack, discovered by online security firm ESET, targeted MEE's website during two days in April 2020. The campaign targeted 20 other websites in two waves: April to July 2020 and January to August 2021. ESET said that the targets had "links to the Middle East and a strong focus on Yemen and the surrounding conflict". Following findings by the two research groups, Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, and other platforms have since disconnected Discover-Tech's access to the digital advertising market. sources.title: How Israeli firm’s ‘zero-click’ malware attack poses global security risk - Al Jazeera
passages: An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims.
Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat.
“We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera.
Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru.

The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries.
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024.
Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed.
Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found.
Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance.
“Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.”
A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part.
The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets.

Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners.

In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.

extraction.body: A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part. Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found. You are not even required to “click” on anything. An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims. In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files. An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks. Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera. “This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.” Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners. Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists , journalists and political activists across 10 countries. Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable. Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera. “To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities. “The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said. Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials. It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time. Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect. While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection. Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on. “Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.” “Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added. Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax. In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse. Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found. The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat. Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab. In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.” The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said. Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

MSCI ( NYSE: MSCI ), a well-known index provider followed by many passive investment funds, plans to classify companies like Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR ) as "non-operating." This change would make them ineligible for MSCI's global indexes. As a result, Strategy could end up on a potential deletions list alongside Japan's Metaplanet, with final decisions expected by November 11, 2026, and removals starting on November 30. After the news, Strategy's stock fell 9.6% to $137 on October 16 and has dropped 11.4% over the past week. Meanwhile, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) remained relatively stable, slipping just 1.0% in the 24 hours leading up to October 16 to $81,548. So, how might this index decision, concerning the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, impact Bitcoin's price? The controversy began with an MSCI proposal that would have excluded any company whose digital asset holdings made up more than 50% of its total assets. Strategy voiced strong opposition, describing this threshold as "discriminatory towards digital assets" and "arbitrary," according to Chief Financial Officer Andrew Kang during a February 5 earnings call. Though MSCI retracted this proposal in January, the provider eventually initiated a broader consultation that led to the current "non-operating assets" test driving the potential removals. Strategy formally opposed the test, with Kang insisting that Strategy is "an operating company with a treasury balance sheet built upon a commodity," highlighting its 1,500-employee workforce and 2025 revenue of $477 million. While the company's software division generates consistent revenue—reporting $122.4 million in the second quarter (up 6.9% from the previous year), with subscription services growing by 54% to $62.9 million—most investors hold shares in Strategy primarily for its Bitcoin assets. The company holds 848,250 BTC, valued at about $69 billion at the current Bitcoin price, exceeding its $55.25 billion market cap. However, the second quarter also posted a substantial net loss of $8.22 billion, mainly due to an $8.32 billion unrealized loss on Bitcoin, as fair value accounting requires the company to mark its holdings to market every quarter. Index funds are passive investments that mirror the holdings of the indexes they track. If Strategy is removed from the index, index funds would be required to sell their shares, which could trigger about $2.8 billion in forced selling, according to JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE: JPM ). While this selling would affect MSTR shares, it wouldn't directly impact Bitcoin. The shares would change hands between buyers and sellers, so Strategy would retain custody of its Bitcoin. Bitcoin prices would only be affected if the company decided to sell some of its holdings, and the current MSCI terms don't obligate any company to do so. Michael Saylor, Strategy's executive chairman, expressed that the MSCI decision is "not that important to us," adding that MSCI manages "a fairly de minimis amount of capital." However, this perspective is expected, given that Saylor represents a company that could lose its index status. Traders, for their part, treated the news as a serious threat. The main link between Strategy's stock and Bitcoin is the company's buying power. Strategy has heavily invested in Bitcoin, funding purchases through the sale of new shares and preferred stock. In the second quarter alone, it raised $8.41 billion through "at-the-market" offerings. In 2025, it raised $25.3 billion. If the stock price declines and fewer index funds hold the shares, raising money could become more challenging. Strategy might need to issue a greater number of shares to acquire the same amount of Bitcoin. Furthermore, with an S&P credit rating of B-, far below investment grade, the company faces higher borrowing costs and limited access to bond funds that only deal in highly rated debt. Additionally, Strategy has recently begun selling some of its Bitcoin. The company's board approved sales of up to $1.25 billion to support its USD Reserve, and it has already sold $218.4 million of Bitcoin this year. The reserve currently stands at $3.75 billion, enough to cover more than 2.1 years of preferred dividends and interest on its $6.7 billion in convertible debt. MSCI ( NYSE: MSCI | MSCI Price Prediction ), a well-known index provider followed by many passive investment funds, plans to classify companies like Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR ) as “non-operating.” This change would make them ineligible for MSCI’s global indexes. As a result, Strategy could end up on a potential deletions list alongside Japan’s Metaplanet, with final decisions expected by November 11, 2026, and removals starting on November 30.

After the news, Strategy’s stock fell 9.6% to $137 on October 16 and has dropped 11.4% over the past week. Meanwhile, Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) remained relatively stable , slipping just 1.0% in the 24 hours leading up to October 16 to $81,548. So, how might this index decision, concerning the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin , impact Bitcoin’s price?

The controversy began with an MSCI proposal that would have excluded any company whose digital asset holdings made up more than 50% of its total assets. Strategy voiced strong opposition, describing this threshold as “discriminatory towards digital assets” and “arbitrary,” according to Chief Financial Officer Andrew Kang during a February 5 earnings call.

Though MSCI retracted this proposal in January, the provider eventually initiated a broader consultation that led to the current “non-operating assets” test driving the potential removals. Strategy formally opposed the test, with Kang insisting that Strategy is “an operating company with a treasury balance sheet built upon a commodity,” highlighting its 1,500-employee workforce and 2025 revenue of $477 million.

While the company’s software division generates consistent revenue—reporting $122.4 million in the second quarter (up 6.9% from the previous year), with subscription services growing by 54% to $62.9 million—most investors hold shares in Strategy primarily for its Bitcoin assets. The company holds 848,250 BTC, valued at about $69 billion at the current Bitcoin price, exceeding its $55.25 billion market cap.

However, the second quarter also posted a substantial net loss of $8.22 billion, mainly due to an $8.32 billion unrealized loss on Bitcoin, as fair value accounting requires the company to mark its holdings to market every quarter.

Index funds are passive investments that mirror the holdings of the indexes they track. If Strategy is removed from the index, index funds would be required to sell their shares, which could trigger about $2.8 billion in forced selling, according to JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE: JPM ).

While this selling would affect MSTR shares, it wouldn’t directly impact Bitcoin. The shares would change hands between buyers and sellers, so Strategy would retain custody of its Bitcoin. Bitcoin prices would only be affected if the company decided to sell some of its holdings, and the current MSCI terms don’t obligate any company to do so.

Michael Saylor, Strategy’s executive chairman, expressed that the MSCI decision is “not that important to us,” adding that MSCI manages “a fairly de minimis amount of capital.” However, this perspective is expected, given that Saylor represents a company that could lose its index status. Traders, for their part, treated the news as a serious threat.

The main link between Strategy’s stock and Bitcoin is the company’s buying power. Strategy has heavily invested in Bitcoin, funding purchases through the sale of new shares and preferred stock. In the second quarter alone, it raised $8.41 billion through “at-the-market” offerings. In 2025, it raised $25.3 billion.

If the stock price declines and fewer index funds hold the shares, raising money could become more challenging. Strategy might need to issue a greater number of shares to acquire the same amount of Bitcoin. Furthermore, with an S&P credit rating of B-, far below investment grade, the company faces higher borrowing costs and limited access to bond funds that only deal in highly rated debt.

Additionally, Strategy has recently begun selling some of its Bitcoin. The company’s board approved sales of up to $1.25 billion to support its USD Reserve, and it has already sold $218.4 million of Bitcoin this year. The reserve currently stands at $3.75 billion, enough to cover more than 2.1 years of preferred dividends and interest on its $6.7 billion in convertible debt.

However, the pressure on Bitcoin prices remains. Strategy’s average purchase price is around $75,444 per Bitcoin, and Bitcoin’s current $81,548 is only about 8% above it, while it trades 35.3% below its record high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. That said, Saylor previously reassured investors that falling below that cost threshold would not trigger any major actions, stating that Strategy has no “covenants or triggers” tied to its purchase price.

The MSCI change is primarily an issue for Strategy’s stock rather than Bitcoin directly. Bitcoin’s price may be affected only if the company significantly slows its buying or decides to sell its Bitcoin assets in the future.

The first clear test comes with MSCI’s final list on November 11. If Strategy is on it and its reports after the November 30 removals show Bitcoin sales beyond the $218.4 million already sold this year, the index exit has reached the coin. If its purchases keep coming instead, the damage stays with MSTR shareholders.

MSCI ( NYSE: MSCI ), a well-known index provider followed by many passive investment funds, plans to classify companies like Strategy Inc. ( NASDAQ: MSTR ) as "non-operating." This change would make them ineligible for MSCI's global indexes. As a result, Strategy could end up on a potential deletions list alongside Japan's Metaplanet, with final decisions expected by November 11, 2026, and removals starting on November 30. After the news, Strategy's stock fell 9.6% to $137 on October 16 and has dropped 11.4% over the past week. Meanwhile, Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) remained relatively stable, slipping just 1.0% in the 24 hours leading up to October 16 to $81,548. So, how might this index decision, concerning the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, impact Bitcoin's price? The controversy began with an MSCI proposal that would have excluded any company whose digital asset holdings made up more than 50% of its total assets. Strategy voiced strong opposition, describing this threshold as "discriminatory towards digital assets" and "arbitrary," according to Chief Financial Officer Andrew Kang during a February 5 earnings call. Though MSCI retracted this proposal in January, the provider eventually initiated a broader consultation that led to the current "non-operating assets" test driving the potential removals. Strategy formally opposed the test, with Kang insisting that Strategy is "an operating company with a treasury balance sheet built upon a commodity," highlighting its 1,500-employee workforce and 2025 revenue of $477 million. While the company's software division generates consistent revenue—reporting $122.4 million in the second quarter (up 6.9% from the previous year), with subscription services growing by 54% to $62.9 million—most investors hold shares in Strategy primarily for its Bitcoin assets. The company holds 848,250 BTC, valued at about $69 billion at the current Bitcoin price, exceeding its $55.25 billion market cap. However, the second quarter also posted a substantial net loss of $8.22 billion, mainly due to an $8.32 billion unrealized loss on Bitcoin, as fair value accounting requires the company to mark its holdings to market every quarter. Index funds are passive investments that mirror the holdings of the indexes they track. If Strategy is removed from the index, index funds would be required to sell their shares, which could trigger about $2.8 billion in forced selling, according to JPMorgan Chase ( NYSE: JPM ). While this selling would affect MSTR shares, it wouldn't directly impact Bitcoin. The shares would change hands between buyers and sellers, so Strategy would retain custody of its Bitcoin. Bitcoin prices would only be affected if the company decided to sell some of its holdings, and the current MSCI terms don't obligate any company to do so. Michael Saylor, Strategy's executive chairman, expressed that the MSCI decision is "not that important to us," adding that MSCI manages "a fairly de minimis amount of capital." However, this perspective is expected, given that Saylor represents a company that could lose its index status. Traders, for their part, treated the news as a serious threat. The main link between Strategy's stock and Bitcoin is the company's buying power. Strategy has heavily invested in Bitcoin, funding purchases through the sale of new shares and preferred stock. In the second quarter alone, it raised $8.41 billion through "at-the-market" offerings. In 2025, it raised $25.3 billion. If the stock price declines and fewer index funds hold the shares, raising money could become more challenging. Strategy might need to issue a greater number of shares to acquire the same amount of Bitcoin. Furthermore, with an S&P credit rating of B-, far below investment grade, the company faces higher borrowing costs and limited access to bond funds that only deal in highly rated debt. Additionally, Strategy has recently begun selling some of its Bitcoin. The company's board approved sales of up to $1.25 billion to support its USD Reserve, and it has already sold $218.4 million of Bitcoin this year. The reserve currently stands at $3.75 billion, enough to cover more than 2.1 years of preferred dividends and interest on its $6.7 billion in convertible debt. However, the pressure on Bitcoin prices remains. Strategy's average purchase price is around $75,444 per Bitcoin, and Bitcoin's current $81,548 is only about 8% above it, while it trades 35.3% below its record high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. That said, Saylor previously reassured investors that falling below that cost threshold would not trigger any major actions, stating that Strategy has no "covenants or triggers" tied to its purchase price. The MSCI change is primarily an issue for Strategy's stock rather than Bitcoin directly. Bitcoin's price may be affected only if the company significantly slows its buying or decides to sell its Bitcoin assets in the future. The first clear test comes with MSCI's final list on November 11. If Strategy is on it and its reports after the November 30 removals show Bitcoin sales beyond the $218.4 million already sold this year, the index exit has reached the coin. However, this perspective is expected, given that Saylor represents a company that could lose its index status. Traders, for their part, treated the news as a serious threat.

In the second quarter alone, it raised $8.41 billion through "at-the-market" offerings. In 2025, it raised $25.3 billion.

If the stock price declines and fewer index funds hold the shares, raising money could become more challenging. Strategy might need to issue a greater number of shares to acquire the same amount of Bitcoin. Furthermore, with an S&P credit rating of B-, far below investment grade, the company faces higher borrowing costs and limited access to bond funds that only deal in highly rated debt.

Additionally, Strategy has recently begun selling some of its Bitcoin. The company's board approved sales of up to $1.25 billion to support its USD Reserve, and it has already sold $218.4 million of Bitcoin this year. The reserve currently stands at $3.75 billion, enough to cover more than 2.1 years of preferred dividends and interest on its $6.7 billion in convertible debt.

However, the pressure on Bitcoin prices remains. Strategy's average purchase price is around $75,444 per Bitcoin, and Bitcoin's current $81,548 is only about 8% above it, while it trades 35.3% below its record high of $126,080 set on October 6, 2025. That said, Saylor previously reassured investors that falling below that cost threshold would not trigger any major actions, stating that Strategy has no "covenants or triggers" tied to its purchase price.

The MSCI change is primarily an issue for Strategy's stock rather than Bitcoin directly. Bitcoin's price may be affected only if the company significantly slows its buying or decides to sell its Bitcoin assets in the future.

passages: Crypto traders often call October "Uptober" because Bitcoin typically finishes the month with gains.
Since 2013, it has closed with losses only twice before 2025: in 2014 and 2018.
However, last year proved the trend could break, as Bitcoin ended October 2025 below its starting price.
Traders tend to buy Bitcoin early in the month when they anticipate an upswing, which can lead to price increases at the start of October.
Conversely, if October begins weakly, those expectations can prompt quick selling, which may push prices down further.
As we reach the midpoint of October 2026, Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) has dropped roughly 4%, putting its annual "Uptober" trend at risk once again.
As of October 12, Bitcoin is trading around $83,400, down from its September close of nearly $87,000.
Ultimately, the Uptober record offers little insight into how October 2026 will end.

A Bitcoin closing price above about $87,000 could keep the Uptober tradition alive for another year, while a close below that would mark a second consecutive October in the red, further diminishing the significance of the "Uptober" label.
Over the past week, every major cryptocurrency has fallen, with Bitcoin down 3%.
Bitcoin's positive months have consistently outnumbered negative months over about a dozen years, contributing to the nickname's popularity.
Moreover, no specific event or trigger in October guarantees strong Bitcoin performance.

Currently, Bitcoin is trading about 23.4% lower than one year ago, highlighting how today’s market feels different for investors.
To regain lost ground, Bitcoin would need to rise about 4.1% from its October 17 price of $81,497 to return to its October 1 open of $84,856 . Several factors have driven its decline this month.

First, forced selling has played a significant role. On October 8, when Bitcoin’s price dipped below $81,000, exchanges liquidated $974 million in cryptocurrency positions, including $896 million in long positions. With the Federal Reserve having raised interest rates in September, market sentiment is influenced by anticipation of its next meeting on October 28. As of October 14, futures traders were pricing in a 47% chance of another rate hike.

Consequently, cumulative net inflows fell from approximately $57.6 billion on October 1 to $56.96 billion by October 15. This contrasts sharply with September, when these funds saw a significant inflow of $999 million on September 21 alone.

While Uptober isn’t officially over, Bitcoin’s chances of finishing the month positively look slim. coreStoryFacts.text: Crypto traders often call October "Uptober" because Bitcoin typically finishes the month with gains.
Since 2013, it has closed with losses only twice before 2025: in 2014 and 2018.
However, last year proved the trend could break, as Bitcoin ended October 2025 below its starting price.
Traders tend to buy Bitcoin early in the month when they anticipate an upswing, which can lead to price increases at the start of October.
Conversely, if October begins weakly, those expectations can prompt quick selling, which may push prices down further.
As we reach the midpoint of October 2026, Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) has dropped roughly 4%, putting its annual "Uptober" trend at risk once again.
As of October 12, Bitcoin is trading around $83,400, down from its September close of nearly $87,000.
Ultimately, the Uptober record offers little insight into how October 2026 will end.

A Bitcoin closing price above about $87,000 could keep the Uptober tradition alive for another year, while a close below that would mark a second consecutive October in the red, further diminishing the significance of the "Uptober" label.
Over the past week, every major cryptocurrency has fallen, with Bitcoin down 3%.
Bitcoin's positive months have consistently outnumbered negative months over about a dozen years, contributing to the nickname's popularity.
Moreover, no specific event or trigger in October guarantees strong Bitcoin performance.

Crypto traders often call October "Uptober" because Bitcoin typically finishes the month with gains. Since 2013, it has closed with losses only twice before 2025: in 2014 and 2018. However, last year proved the trend could break, as Bitcoin ended October 2025 below its starting price. So, what does this record mean for the remainder of October 2026? Is "Uptober" just a catchy name, or is there more to it? The impressive record of positive October performances has garnered attention over the years. Bitcoin's positive months have consistently outnumbered negative months over about a dozen years, contributing to the nickname's popularity. However, a dozen October performances is still a small sample size, and a single October loss, like in 2025, can significantly alter this pattern. Small samples can look more significant than they really are, as a few strong years can create trends that may not hold over time. Moreover, no specific event or trigger in October guarantees strong Bitcoin performance. In contrast, scheduled events like token unlocks can directly affect supply. A calendar change alone does not provide a clear incentive for buyers. Many successful investors eventually reach the same moment. Traders tend to buy Bitcoin early in the month when they anticipate an upswing, which can lead to price increases at the start of October. Conversely, if October begins weakly, those expectations can prompt quick selling, which may push prices down further. This self-reinforcing cycle can weaken the reliability of the Uptober forecast. Over the past week, every major cryptocurrency has fallen, with Bitcoin down 3%. Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) fell 6%, XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) fell 7.3%, Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) fell 7.6%, and Dogecoin (CRYPTO:DOGE) fell 9.7%. Interestingly, the extent of each coin's drop reflects trader behavior. passages: The shooting happened around 2 a.m. on March 15 at 1900 East Long Ave.According to the affidavit filed by Fort Worth police, Parish was a passenger in a black 2004 Ford Expedition and had been firing a tan handgun into the ground several times before the encounter. Investigators say Avila, who reportedly appeared intoxicated and possibly having a schizophrenic episode, approached the SUV at the intersection of East Long and Schwartz avenues because he was upset that Parish had been firing a weapon in the neighborhood.Witnesses and occupants of the vehicle told police that Avila was unarmed and stood on the left side of the SUV, yelling at Parish through the passenger window.

The shooting happened around 2 a.m. on March 15 at 1900 East Long Ave.According to the affidavit filed by Fort Worth police, Parish was a passenger in a black 2004 Ford Expedition and had been firing a tan handgun into the ground several times before the encounter. Investigators say Avila, who reportedly appeared intoxicated and possibly having a schizophrenic episode, approached the SUV at the intersection of East Long and Schwartz avenues because he was upset that Parish had been firing a weapon in the neighborhood.Witnesses and occupants of the vehicle told police that Avila was unarmed and stood on the left side of the SUV, yelling at Parish through the passenger window. When the driver reversed and tried to drive around Avila, he moved into the vehicle's path, forcing it to stop again.As Avila walked toward the front of the vehicle, the affidavit alleges that Parish stuck the tan pistol out of the window and fired one shot. Avila collapsed in a grassy median and died at the scene.The occupants of the vehicle initially left the scene but then made a U-turn to return and check if the man had been shot. Officers, alerted by the Real Time Crime Center, conducted an investigatory stop in the 2900 block of North Nichols and detained all five people inside the vehicle. Police found a black pistol and a tan pistol in plain view inside the vehicle.The investigating detective noted that no witnesses believed Avila was armed or attempting to assault anyone, saying Parish used deadly force despite not being threatened with imminent harm.Parish remains in custody on a murder charge.

According to Fort Worth Police, an armed security guard working inside the shopping center was nearby as the man smashed glass display cases. At some point during the incident, a security guard working at the shopping center encountered the man. "As the male was smashing the glass casing, at some point, the security guard fired his weapon at the male, striking him at least one time. The details surrounding the shooting are still being investigated," Fort Worth Police Department spokesperson Officer Buddy Calzada said during a late-night briefing. Create a free account with NBC 5 DFW to save articles and videos. Police said the man ran out of the shopping center, crossed the parking lot and collapsed near Seminary Drive. extraction.body: The man who shot another while on duty as a security guard at a Fort Worth shopping center has been arrested for murder, police said. 31-year-old Tyron Henton was arrested on Oct. 16 and charged with murder in connection with a shooting at the La Gran Plaza shopping center in the 4200 block of South Freeway. According to Fort Worth Police, an armed security guard working inside the shopping center was nearby as the man smashed glass display cases. At some point during the incident, a security guard working at the shopping center encountered the man. "As the male was smashing the glass casing, at some point, the security guard fired his weapon at the male, striking him at least one time. The details surrounding the shooting are still being investigated," Fort Worth Police Department spokesperson Officer Buddy Calzada said during a late-night briefing. Create a free account with NBC 5 DFW to save articles and videos. Police said the man ran out of the shopping center, crossed the parking lot and collapsed near Seminary Drive. Officers and Fort Worth firefighters arriving at the scene found the man and began lifesaving measures, including CPR. He was pronounced dead at the scene by medical personnel. According to the hours posted on the plaza's website, La Gran Plaza was open at the time of the incident but was preparing to close at 9 p.m.

extraction.body: Millbrook Magnet High School had a very unexpected and special delivery on Thursday morning after the school's security officer went into labor. Principal Monica Sawyer and bookkeeper K'Mani Freeman heard the call for help and quickly jumped into action. "We got a call go out on our radios that said that there was a medical emergency in one of our bathrooms," Sawyer said. Freeman says she’s a Douala and instructed the principal what to do. She says the baby arrived within minutes. "I was like, well, we have a baby. Great, we probably need to warm her up just a little bit," Freeman said. Sawyer said it's a moment she'll never forget. "I heard a baby was crying and Ms. Freeman was telling us to go get a blanket from our office," Sawyer said. "I thought Brook would be a beautiful name as an ode to Millbrook. But we don't know. Mom hasn't decided yet," Sawyer said. In a letter to staff and families, Principal Sawyer said school staff stepped in to help deliver a beautiful baby girl on campus that morning. "We’re happy to share that both mom and baby are doing well," Sawyer said. "I know you’ll join me in congratulating the family and welcoming our newest (and tiniest!) Wildcat. We’ve already ordered some baby spirit wear so mom and daughter will be ready to cheer on the Wildcats together!" The school has set up a page to help support the newborn and family at this link. "What a special day to be a Wildcat!" Sawyer said.

passages: At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did.
As part of updates announced Friday, Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps.
Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved.
The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors.

extraction.body: Apple’s App Store rules now more explicitly ban so-called “nudify” apps that generate intimate images of people without their consent using AI tools. The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors. Apple didn’t pull X or Grok from the App Store, though it told senators that it threatened to yank Grok. At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did. As part of updates announced Friday, Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps. Developers who “fail to implement adequate safeguards” or “don’t remedy violations after notice” may be removed from the App Store. Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved. Apple’s rules also more clearly spell out that any apps that “facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children” will be pulled from the App Store and “blocked from alternative distribution.”

passages: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents.

sources.body: This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. In July, OpenAI’s agents escaped a test environment and hacked French company Hugging Face — kicking off a summer of rogue AI agent activity. Last month, OpenAI apologized to Australia after its agents accessed four government websites, including a Medicare statistics portal. At Hugging Face, OpenAI’s agents started the same way but then found and exploited software flaws to run code on the company’s servers. CERT-In described no such hacking in India, where the agents appear to have simply used the access left lying around. Still, the Indian cases appear to be worse in one respect, which is what the agents saw: In Australia, OpenAI said it found no evidence its agents touched individuals’ medical or criminal records, even after they wrote files inside a Medicare statistics system, while in India, agents read personal data and confidential business records. And unlike earlier incidents, each disclosed by a single lab, India’s case involved agents from multiple providers. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations, or say whether the agents altered any systems. TechCrunch has reached out to CERT-In for more information. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. The disclosures have left governments relying on AI companies causing these breaches to voluntarily disclose rogue AI agent activity. passages: Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors.
Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images.
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

extraction.body: Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way. Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy. The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role. “It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.” That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking. “I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.” When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea. “I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.” He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness. “I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. “It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.”
That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking.

“I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.”

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

“I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.”
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

“I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.”

sources.pageTitle: Tesla turns to 50-year-old stunt technology as it tries to Roadster again - Ars Technica

sources.title: Tesla turns to 50-year-old stunt technology as it tries to Roadster again
passages: Nine years after first trying to resurrect the Roadster , Tesla is apparently trying again.

CEO Elon Musk might have relocated its HQ to Texas, but yet again he has returned to California’s showbiz industry to hawk his wares; last time it was a Hollywood back lot for the remote-controlled Cybercab demo , last night it was decades-old stunt technology to make a show car do tricks in the air.
And right now, that’s the McMurtry Spéirling, which looks like a miniaturized Batmobile (the good Michael Keaton one) and which is capable of generating up to 3.5 lateral Gs.
The best Tesla claims for the new Roadster is 2 Gs.
Oh, and the Spéirling will most definitely drive upside down.
Musk claims that the Roadster will go into production by 2028.

But the CEO has a long and glorious history of overpromising and underdelivering; in 2017 he told attendees at the previous launch that “We are making it now.” Using the company’s referral program, some people were in line to receive two free cars.
But those free cars never showed up, and neither did the ones that people put down $50,000 deposits for; last year Sam Altman discovered how hard it can be to get that money back .
But as Musk has told us time and again, Tesla is no longer a car company .
Currently, he seems more interested in merging Tesla with SpaceX , claiming synergies having to do with AI despite most of his AI-derived revenues coming from renting GPU time to others.
But a merger would give SpaceX a backdoor into the S&P 500 index, which rejected the rocket company in June, as it requires several consecutive profitable quarters for inclusion.
Apparently, that could happen before the end of the year.
At the rear are four giant exhaust pipes; these do not signal Tesla’s sudden embrace of hydrocarbons beyond those emitted by private aviation.

The battery pack uses the troubled 4680 cells it has been trying to scale up in-house; customer complaints of poor performance were presumably the driving force behind developing what the company says is a special battery chemistry just for this model.
Some of the performance claims are even more grandiose than nine years ago.
Now, Musk claims a planned top speed of 383 mph (616 km/h), with a 0-60 mph time of 0.8 seconds.
And as with the last time this happened , there are already other EVs on sale that are more capable than Tesla’s vaporware claims.

Its stratospheric valuation was predicated in large part upon promises of constant growth, something that perhaps seemed possible when its market share was near total and there was little competition for EVs.
But now Europe and China have hundreds of models to choose from—only two of which are offered by Tesla.
The Models 3 and Y are both increasingly aged, and Tesla has shown little ability to innovate rapidly like the Chinese brands that have taken so much of its sales away there.
In fact, it might even leave the Chinese market .
Meanwhile, Tesla’s core business remains in trouble.
Even in quarters with decent sales, its profits are vanishing as costs rise and selling prices drop .
And most recently, sales have not been decent .

The new Roadster, we’re told, will be unlike anything else, although the angular, wedge-shaped styling owes more than a little to Giorgetto Giugiaro’s original Lotus Esprit—Musk is known to own a James Bond prop car—as well as the more recent Lamborghini Gallardo. At the rear are four giant exhaust pipes; these do not signal Tesla’s sudden embrace of hydrocarbons beyond those emitted by private aviation. Rather, it’s where 100,000 psi jets of compressed nitrogen shoot out. It’s early in the morning and the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Statutes are dense reading, so I am yet to find the section where it explains how and when it’s legal to use such a thing on the road. Unusually, Tesla says it stuck with rear-wheel drive for the new electric vehicle. The battery pack uses the troubled 4680 cells it has been trying to scale up in-house; customer complaints of poor performance were presumably the driving force behind developing what the company says is a special battery chemistry just for this model. Some of the performance claims are even more grandiose than nine years ago. Now, Musk claims a planned top speed of 383 mph (616 km/h), with a 0-60 mph time of 0.8 seconds. And as with the last time this happened , there are already other EVs on sale that are more capable than Tesla’s vaporware claims. And right now, that’s the McMurtry Spéirling, which looks like a miniaturized Batmobile (the good Michael Keaton one) and which is capable of generating up to 3.5 lateral Gs. The best Tesla claims for the new Roadster is 2 Gs. Oh, and the Spéirling will most definitely drive upside down. The Spéirling has also set a faster lap time around the Top Gear test track than an F1 car, blitzed the Goodwood Hill Climb record, and I’m pretty sure would demolish Volkswagen’s untouchable Pikes Peak time if it gave it a shot. McMurtry has sold at least 24 of the planned 100-car production run. Musk claims that the Roadster will go into production by 2028. But the CEO has a long and glorious history of overpromising and underdelivering; in 2017 he told attendees at the previous launch that “We are making it now.” Using the company’s referral program, some people were in line to receive two free cars. But those free cars never showed up, and neither did the ones that people put down $50,000 deposits for; last year Sam Altman discovered how hard it can be to get that money back . And it’s not like there’s actually much of a market for very expensive, very fast EVs: hypercar buyers want noise and an emotional connection, and they don’t get that from an EV . Meanwhile, Tesla’s core business remains in trouble. Even in quarters with decent sales, its profits are vanishing as costs rise and selling prices drop . And most recently, sales have not been decent . Its stratospheric valuation was predicated in large part upon promises of constant growth, something that perhaps seemed possible when its market share was near total and there was little competition for EVs. But now Europe and China have hundreds of models to choose from—only two of which are offered by Tesla. The Models 3 and Y are both increasingly aged, and Tesla has shown little ability to innovate rapidly like the Chinese brands that have taken so much of its sales away there. In fact, it might even leave the Chinese market . But as Musk has told us time and again, Tesla is no longer a car company . Currently, he seems more interested in merging Tesla with SpaceX , claiming synergies having to do with AI despite most of his AI-derived revenues coming from renting GPU time to others. But a merger would give SpaceX a backdoor into the S&P 500 index, which rejected the rocket company in June, as it requires several consecutive profitable quarters for inclusion. Should Musk succeed, he will have access to billions of dollars from passive investment funds that invest retirement accounts in the S&P 500. Apparently, that could happen before the end of the year. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” In the other incident , a model instructed to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard bypassed the organization’s security controls and used the unauthorized access to steal credentials. It then made configuration changes on the server. In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. “The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration,” OpenAI said. “All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.” In a third report , the company said a model prompted to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a locked wallet on a test network. The model “derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment.” The report continued: “The model questioned whether it had permission, then reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. The deployment succeeded and charged transaction fees to the account. This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization.” In the last report , OpenAI said that a model bypassed restrictions researchers had placed on the types of web requests it could make. During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics. OpenAI went on: After finding a public yearbook and submitting an answer, it continued probing for another route to the statistics service. It caused an external browser to send POST requests, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. It then developed a reusable helper that returned response text through a forwarding service and callback mailbox, repeatedly checked the retrieved figures, and used saved data in submitted responses. This case shows how a model can bypass restrictions on its own tools by getting external services to perform the blocked actions, even after finding another way to answer the question. The model first tried to use an external browser with permission to make GET requests on its behalf, then used JavaScript to obtain the information. The model then used an online mailbox to troubleshoot the technique. Eventually, the model settled on a different method: It asked the external browser to open a web form that sent the trade query to the statistics service by POST. When the browser displayed the response, a rendering service returned a GIF image of the page. The model then used optical character recognition to read the figures from the image. It has become common for researchers and journalists to describe incidents like these as AI “going rogue.” That’s not necessarily true. While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads. Further, most or all of the models had disabled certain guardrails that might have prevented the actions. In this sense, the models performed precisely as OpenAI had trained them to. In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly.

In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said .
“It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied.

extraction.body: The actions could have resulted in criminal charges had humans been behind the keyboard. OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” In the other incident , a model instructed to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard bypassed the organization’s security controls and used the unauthorized access to steal credentials. It then made configuration changes on the server. In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. “The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration,” OpenAI said. “All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.” In a third report , the company said a model prompted to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a locked wallet on a test network. The model “derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment.” The report continued: “The model questioned whether it had permission, then reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. The deployment succeeded and charged transaction fees to the account. This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization.” In the last report , OpenAI said that a model bypassed restrictions researchers had placed on the types of web requests it could make. During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics. OpenAI went on: After finding a public yearbook and submitting an answer, it continued probing for another route to the statistics service. It caused an external browser to send POST requests, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. It then developed a reusable helper that returned response text through a forwarding service and callback mailbox, repeatedly checked the retrieved figures, and used saved data in submitted responses. This case shows how a model can bypass restrictions on its own tools by getting external services to perform the blocked actions, even after finding another way to answer the question. The model first tried to use an external browser with permission to make GET requests on its behalf, then used JavaScript to obtain the information. The model then used an online mailbox to troubleshoot the technique. Eventually, the model settled on a different method: It asked the external browser to open a web form that sent the trade query to the statistics service by POST. When the browser displayed the response, a rendering service returned a GIF image of the page. The model then used optical character recognition to read the figures from the image. It has become common for researchers and journalists to describe incidents like these as AI “going rogue.” That’s not necessarily true. While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads. Further, most or all of the models had disabled certain guardrails that might have prevented the actions. In this sense, the models performed precisely as OpenAI had trained them to. sources.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia building non-negotiable ‘security zone’ inside Ukrainian border, Putin declares - The Guardian
passages: Russia is establishing a “security zone” inside Ukraine along the border and it will be non-negotiable in any ⁠future talks with Kyiv, Vladimir Putin has said .

The Russian president, wearing military uniform and speaking during a visit to a command post, said the operation ⁠was in response to Ukraine’s ⁠2024-25 incursion into ​Russia’s western Kursk region .
This task is being carried out successfully,” he said in televised comments on Friday.
“Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions ⁠for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with ​Ukraine.”
The planned ‌security zone spanned 660km (410 ‌miles) , of which 70% was currently under Russia’s control, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.
Peskov did not say how deep it would ‌reach inside Ukraine.
The zone requires Russia to carve out land in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, which are not among those it is illegally claiming as its own territory.

Zelenskyy said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service had not yet been fully restored , as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.
Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels and asked the EU for another €70bn ($79bn/£59bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia, report Jennifer Rankin and Andrew Roth .
Hours earlier Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” after his purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
The attacks came as a new report showed that civilian casualties from Russia’s invasion have climbed steeply.
At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded last month – a total that is 85% higher than in September last year, the report from the UN human rights office in Kyiv said on Friday.
It said intensifying Russian attacks in October already had killed dozens of civilians, including children.
“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, the UN office head.

As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian, writes Andrew Roth in this analysis .
Two were kiled and 12 more wounded in attacks on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, governor Oleh Syniehubov ⁠said.
Further Russian strikes through the evening injured nine, officials said.
A Russian ⁠airstrike on ​Kherson in southern ⁠Ukraine killed one ⁠person ​and ‌injured ‌19 others , the governor ‌said on Saturday.
The person ‌killed was an ​ambulance driver and ⁠a child ​was among the ​injured, ​Oleksandr Prokudin ​said ‌on ​Telegram.

extraction.body: Aisata Diallo, 24, calls herself a lifelong braider. “I’ve always braided my hair growing up and, at some point in my college career, started braiding other people’s hair,” she said. At Northeastern University in Boston, she found limited access to braiders and textured-hair specialists, so she decided to fill that gap by starting a small business of her own. “Throughout that experience, I was very close to some of the pain points in the styling process and complained about it constantly,” she said. Braiding is a manual task, and a single style can take eight hours to complete. Many professionals deal with issues like cramping and carpal tunnel syndrome after spending long days standing behind a chair weaving hair into patterns. At first, Diallo said she didn’t know what to do about it. “I stopped braiding, and one of the reasons that I stopped braiding was due to the physical toll it has on your body.” She wanted to find a way to make braiding less painful and wondered whether new AI technology could automate some part of the process. Building hardware for braiding is expensive, difficult, and complex, which is one reason there have been few innovations in this space. The textured hair market has also long been overlooked by the mainstream. Then, last year, she had an idea: Tressfecta, a company building products for textured hair. Its first project is a tool called Plait Pilot that helps braiders with the initial process of separating hair from packs before braiding begins. That process alone can take hours, especially when a client wants small braids. Diallo said the device is designed to work like this: A stylist places the braiding hair on top of it and sets the size they want the hair separated into, and the device separates the pieces and dispenses them back to the stylist so they can grab them while braiding. “It’s very challenging to build this kind of tool in this space,” she said, citing the nuance and complexity of the braiding style process. Different types of textured hair also need to be accounted for, especially when length and density are considered. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all solution.” Tressfecta is still technically prelaunch, and it is working on the prototype of Plait Pilot. Diallo has been bootstrapping the company, while also drawing on funding from grant and accelerator programs. “I am preparing to fundraise,” she said, noting how hard it can be to raise money for hardware, especially beauty hardware. For now, Diallo said she’s connecting with stylists and braiders who can test the technology. She also spent this week in San Francisco as one of TechCrunch’s Startup Battlefield 200 companies. She doesn’t remember exactly where she first heard about TechCrunch Disrupt, possibly on LinkedIn or in a founder resource group, but when we talked ahead of the show, which wrapped up on Thursday , she was looking forward to connecting with people and showing off her product. She was especially excited to connect with people and for others to see her product. “It feels like a great opportunity,” she said.
